items.title: 68642_Jo Jones oral history interview
items.q: JAMES: Pinetop Smith. [INTERVIEWEE] Leroy Carr, the greatest blues singer that ever lived.

ctx.x: my band? And he played one tune. He played the tune and when he set down at the piano and the minute he put his hands on the piano - just like Fats Waller, plump! - the whole thing settled. He played "From Outer Space" and when Bennie Moten sat down that's the only time I heard piano. I didn't hear no piano from Basie and Bus. They was too busy drinking and hanging out with chicks. Bennie said, "You can't do that to me." And Bennie would come left field. He'd sit down and say, "All right, fellows." And when he…

Well, Basie was mostly the outcome of this because this thing he followed through, just like you say Freddie Greene followed through with the guitar player, Cliff McTyre. Basie must have followed through from the Motens. style and the format of the movements. JAMES: In spiritual values. H: Certainly when we heard the bands, we heard all of you. It was so synonymous that we just considered it more or less a quartet. They are known for the history, for the record, some records - I remember hearing some of them - of…

Now here it is 1973 and fate has it that the only one of you in all that time, which is quite unusual for a rhythm section - only one of you has been lost to - given to the ages and that was Walter Page. So tell me a little about him because he's not here to speak. I can ask Basie
